Union Printing for Political Campaigns: Why It Matters and How to Get It Right

In This Article

  • Who Checks for the Union Bug
  • The Practical Requirements for Union-Label Campaign Printing
  • Campaign Mail Timing in the Hudson Valley
  • The Full Campaign Mail Package at Cornerstone
  • Voter File Targeting for Campaign Mail
  • Multi-Piece Campaign Mail Sequences
  • Campaign Mail Design Essentials

Every election cycle, candidates learn the union bug lesson the hard way: they show up to a union endorsement hearing with a piece of campaign literature — well-designed, professionally printed, and missing the union bug. The labor committee chair asks about it. The candidate wasn’t aware their printer wasn’t union-affiliated. The conversation changes.

The union bug is not a large graphic element. It’s a small, 1/4-inch imprint in the corner of the piece. But its presence or absence tells an organized labor audience something immediate about how seriously the candidate takes labor values in practice, not just in speeches.

At Cornerstone Services in New Paltz, we’ve produced union-label campaign materials for Hudson Valley political campaigns for over 28 years. Here’s what campaigns need to get right.

Who Checks for the Union Bug

Union endorsement committees. Labor organizations in the Hudson Valley — building trades councils, CSEA locals, healthcare worker unions, teachers’ unions, Teamster locals — have endorsement processes that examine whether the candidate’s campaign is practicing labor solidarity. A stack of non-union-printed literature at an endorsement presentation is a concrete example of not doing so.

Union member campaign workers. Campaign volunteers who are union members notice the bug (or its absence) on the materials they’re asked to distribute. The absence creates a credibility problem that is harder to address in conversation than it is to prevent.

Opposition research. In competitive races, opposition campaigns have used the absence of the union bug as a contrast message with union-household voters. “Candidate X says they support workers, but their campaign material was printed non-union” is a specific, verifiable criticism.

News coverage. In local races with labor coverage, the union-label status of campaign materials occasionally appears in reporting. This is rare but not zero.

The Practical Requirements for Union-Label Campaign Printing

Confirm Union Affiliation Before Ordering

Ask any print shop you’re considering: “Are you union-affiliated? What local? Can you provide documentation?”

A union shop will provide the union local name and number immediately, often offer a letter from the local confirming affiliation, and apply the correct bug format to your piece.

A shop that hedges, cannot name a specific local, or says “our workers have the option to join a union” is not union-affiliated in the way endorsement committees mean.

Include the Union Bug in Your Design Specifications

Tell your designer or the print shop at the start of the project: “This needs to carry the union bug.” Do not assume it will be added automatically. The specific bug format (which local, standard language) comes from the print shop — they know which local applies to their shop and what the bug looks like.

The bug typically appears:

  • In the lower right or left corner of the front face
  • Adjacent to the paid-for-by statement
  • In a non-competing location that doesn’t obscure the design

Placement Near Legal Disclosures

New York campaign materials must include paid-for-by attribution. Federal campaign materials (congressional races) must include specific FEC disclaimer language. The conventional placement groups these together in the imprint area:

Paid for by [Campaign Committee Name]
[Union Bug]  [Printer Name, City]

This grouping makes the union affiliation immediately visible to anyone who examines the imprint area, which is exactly where endorsement committee members and informed union voters look.

Campaign Mail Timing in the Hudson Valley

Hudson Valley political races — state assembly, state senate, county legislature, town board — follow a primary calendar (June) and general election calendar (November). Campaign mail has specific timing requirements:

Primary campaigns: Mail planning should begin in late March/early April for a June primary. Marketing Mail takes 3–10 days for delivery in the Hudson Valley; the mailing must drop no later than 10 days before the required in-home date.

General election campaigns: The critical window is October 1–25 for standard campaign mail. Mail dropping after October 20 runs risk of arriving after Election Day.

For campaigns with hard delivery deadlines (a piece must be in mailboxes before a specific event or debate), use First-Class mail rather than Marketing Mail — the 2–5 day delivery window is significantly more predictable.

The Full Campaign Mail Package at Cornerstone

We provide union-label printing for Hudson Valley political campaigns including:

  • Postcards (5.5x8.5, 6x9, EDDM format): The most common format for broad voter outreach, with union bug and paid-for-by imprint
  • Canvass walk sheets and door hangers: Distributed by volunteers, typically not mailed

Voter File Targeting for Campaign Mail

Effective campaign mail reaches the right voters — not just every address on a route. Campaign mail strategy typically involves one or more of these targeting approaches:

Registered voter file (all registered voters): For nonpartisan or broad-appeal campaigns, mailing to all registered voters within the district is the most comprehensive approach. The voter file is available from the county Board of Elections and includes name, address, party registration, and voting history.

Party-targeted voter file: For primary campaigns, mail only to registered members of the candidate’s party. For general election campaigns, target persuadable voters — registered voters in the opposite party who have low primary participation, or enrolled independents.

High-propensity voters: Target voters who have voted in at least 2 of the last 4 elections. These voters are most likely to vote again and most receptive to campaign messaging. This is the most cost-effective targeting approach for campaigns with limited budgets.

Voter suppression is not mail suppression. Targeting specific voter segments for your mail is standard campaign practice. It’s about efficiency — reaching the voters most likely to respond to your message — not about preventing anyone from voting.

At Cornerstone, we process voter file mailings for campaign clients using the same CASS and NCOA processing, inkjet addressing, and presort optimization that we apply to all direct mail. The union bug on the campaign piece and the professional quality of the mailing service combine to present a campaign that appears organized, labor-aligned, and serious.

Multi-Piece Campaign Mail Sequences

Most successful campaign mail programs involve 3–5 mail pieces in a planned sequence over 4–6 weeks before Election Day:

Piece 1 (6 weeks out): Introduction. Who the candidate is, primary qualifications, and the one-sentence reason they’re running. This is the broad awareness piece — sent to the full target universe.

Piece 2 (4 weeks out): Issues/platform. The candidate’s position on the 2–3 issues most important to the district. This piece is more detailed and can be segmented — different messaging for different voter segments if budget allows.

Piece 3 (3 weeks out): Endorsements and social proof. Union endorsements, community leader endorsements, and constituent testimonials. This is where the union bug is especially visible — a piece announcing a labor endorsement that carries the union bug reinforces the message.

Piece 4 (10–14 days out): Contrast/comparison. For competitive races, a contrast piece that compares the candidate’s record or positions to the opponent’s. This piece must be factual — verifiable claims only — and must include the legally required paid-for-by attribution.

Piece 5 (5–7 days out): GOTV (Get Out The Vote). A simple, urgent reminder to vote. Date, polling location, hours. Often a smaller postcard format to keep cost low. Sent to high-propensity supporters identified through the campaign’s voter contact program.

Each piece in the sequence is printed with the union bug when the campaign is pursuing or holding a labor endorsement. The consistency reinforces the labor message across the entire campaign mail program.

Campaign Mail Design Essentials

Political campaign mail pieces have specific design requirements beyond standard commercial printing:

Paid-for-by attribution. New York Election Law requires all political advertising to include a “Paid for by [committee name]” attribution. This must be legible — typically minimum 8 pt. type — and visible on the piece. The attribution, union bug, and postal indicia compete for space in the imprint area, so layout planning is important.

Clear candidate identification. The candidate’s name should be the largest text on the piece. Voters receiving 5–10 political mail pieces per week during campaign season spend 2–3 seconds deciding whether to read or discard each one. The candidate name and a brief message visible at a glance determine whether the piece gets read.

Consistent branding across all pieces. The campaign’s color palette, logo, and typography should be identical across every mail piece in the sequence. Consistency builds recognition — by the third or fourth piece, voters recognize the campaign’s mail before reading it.

High-quality photography. A professional headshot of the candidate and authentic local photography outperform stock images. Voters respond to candidates who look real and relatable, not polished and artificial.

Call to action. Every campaign mail piece should tell the voter what to do: vote on a specific date, attend a rally, visit the campaign website, or call a phone number. A piece without a clear action item is informational but not motivational.

The best campaign mail combines union certification with professional design and strategic messaging. When voters receive a well-designed piece with a clear union bug, they see a campaign that is organized, labor-aligned, and committed to the working people of the district.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do political campaigns use union printing?

Political campaigns use union printing primarily when seeking endorsements from labor organizations or campaigning in districts with significant union household density. Labor unions examine campaign literature as part of their endorsement process — materials produced without the union bug can be disqualifying for endorsements and signal to union members that the candidate does not prioritize labor values in practice. In districts where union households represent 15–30% of reliable voters, this endorsement and signaling effect can be decisive.

What does political campaign printing legally need to include?

Political campaign printed materials in New York must include a 'paid for by' statement identifying the committee or individual paying for the piece. Federal candidates (congressional races) must also include specific disclaimer language required by the FEC. The union bug, while not legally required, is typically placed near the paid-for-by statement in the imprint area. Candidates should confirm all required legal disclosures with their campaign counsel before printing.

Can campaign direct mail be both union-printed and USPS-presorted?

Yes. Union printing applies to the print production phase. USPS presort mailing services are administrative and postal compliance functions that are not subject to union labor requirements. A campaign can print their direct mail at a union shop, then use any qualified mail house (union or non-union) for addressing, presort, and USPS drop. Alternatively, a print shop that also offers mailing services can handle both under one roof — but the mailing services component is not union-specific.

What is the fastest a union print shop can turn around campaign mail?

Rush campaign printing turnaround varies by shop, job size, and scheduling availability. At Cornerstone Services, rush turnaround for standard postcard quantities (2,500–10,000 pieces) is typically 3–5 business days from proof approval. For campaigns with hard deadlines (USPS mail date must be by a specific date), we work backward from the required in-home date: Marketing Mail takes 3–10 days to deliver, so the mailing must drop at USPS no later than 10 days before the required in-home date.
